nameStory: The Cornfield Bolas Spider gets its name from its unique hunting weapon - a sticky droplet of silk dangled on a line that resembles a bolas, the weighted ball-and-rope tool used by South American gauchos to catch livestock. The 'cornfield' part likely refers to agricultural areas where these spiders were first commonly observed hunting moths attracted to crop fields.
description: This is one of nature's most cunning hunters - a small orb weaver that has abandoned traditional web-building for chemical warfare. Instead of spinning webs, the female Cornfield Bolas Spider dangles a sticky silk ball to snare prey, but the real trick is her ability to mimic moth pheromones to lure unsuspecting male moths within striking distance. These spiders are typically small and compact, with females being larger than males, though exact size measurements for this species are not well documented.

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Watch for a spider dangling a sticky droplet on a silk line while releasing chemical attractants - no traditional web present

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, rounded body typical of orb weavers but noticeably stockier than web-building relatives

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: No circular orb web - instead produces a single silk line with a sticky glob at the end

idTips.label: Hunting Time
idTips.description: Most active at night when male moths are flying and can be chemically attracted

habitat: Agricultural areas, field edges, and open woodlands where moths are abundant. Look for them on shrubs, fence posts, or other elevated perches near cornfields, meadows, or areas with night-flying insects. They prefer spots with good air circulation to help disperse their chemical attractants.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging and establishing hunting territories as moth populations increase with warmer weather.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adult females are actively hunting and mating, easily observed on warm nights.
seasonality.fall: Egg-laying occurs and adults may still be active until first hard frosts reduce moth prey availability.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically die off, overwintering as eggs or possibly young spiders in protected locations.

funFact: This spider is essentially a master perfumer - she can change her chemical 'recipe' to mimic different moth species' pheromones, switching her scent profile like a predator changing disguises to target whatever moths are flying that night!
confusionNotes: With only one confirmed sighting in New England, this species is most likely to be confused with other small orb weavers. The key difference is the complete absence of a traditional circular web - if you see a compact spider with a single silk line and sticky droplet, you've likely found a bolas spider.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called an 'orb weaver,' bolas spiders have evolved completely away from web-building, representing one of the most dramatic behavioral shifts in spider evolution. The single New England record suggests this is at the very northern edge of their range.
compareHints: Among the American bolas spiders, the Cornfield Bolas Spider is distinguished by its northern range extension into New England, while most relatives like the Toadlike Bolas Spider are found in more southern regions. All bolas spiders share the same basic hunting strategy but may target different moth species with their chemical mimicry.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Toadlike Bolas Spider can be distinguished from other Mastophora species primarily by its particularly warty, toad-like appearance and geographic range.
Among the bolas spiders, Yeargan's species is distinguished from its relatives primarily by geographic range and subtle differences in body proportions and coloration that require expert examination.
Among the bolas spider relatives, Mastophora bisaccata is distinguished by specific details in body structure and genetic markers that require expert identification.
Mastophora timuqua differs from its bolas spider relatives primarily in geographic distribution, as most other Mastophora species are found further south and west.
**[UNCERTAIN CLAIM]** Stowe's Bolas Spider likely differs from other Mastophora species primarily in its geographic range and possibly the specific moth pheromones it produces.
